strengths: Addresses important and underexplored practical problem: shelf life and deployment concerns of finetuned LLM judges
Clean conceptual framework: dual-distribution formulation elegantly separates question and response distributions for systematic analysis
Rigorous experimental design with thoughtful controls (avoiding self-bias, consistent accuracy metric, multiple evaluation splits)
Comprehensive scope within domain: three base models × three training recipes with detailed ablations and reproducibility information
Clear, well-supported empirical findings: universal failure at future-proofing, DPO superiority, asymmetry between forward/backward compatibility
Well-organized presentation with effective visualizations and clear writing making work accessible
weaknesses: Severely limited scope: entire study restricted to mathematics domain only; no evidence findings generalize to coding, instruction-following, or other evaluation tasks
Limited methodological novelty: dual-distribution formulation is straightforward notation; continual learning is vanilla fine-tuning without exploration of replay/regularization approaches
Shallow mechanistic insights: paper is primarily descriptive, identifying problems without explaining why judges fail or what properties enable robustness
Oversimplified generator strength characterization: binary weak/strong split based only on pass@1; Figure 7 shows ambiguous clustering with substantial overlap
Incomplete continual learning investigation: only DPO evaluated (others dropped for compute reasons), single epoch of training, mixed model-dependent results without principled analysis
Limited practical guidance: main takeaway (regularly retrain on new outputs) is unsurprising; no proposed solutions or mitigations beyond retraining
Methodological concerns: GPT-4o teacher model introduces external dependency; missing batch size/training details; no statistical significance testing; single dataset without cross-dataset validation
Question generalization findings somewhat obvious: overfitting to seen questions is expected without deeper analysis of failure modes or interpolation vs. extrapolation

strengths: Addresses practical and underexplored deployment concerns for finetuned LLM judges
Clean dual-distribution framework that elegantly decomposes question and response distribution shifts
Comprehensive experimental setup spanning three base models, three training recipes, and weak/strong generator tiers
Well-defined metrics (FutureProof, RefreshAdvantage, BackCompatibility, CompatibilityShift) with clear interpretations
Systematic and transparent experimental design with clear presentation of empirical findings
Demonstrates consistent patterns across models and training methods
weaknesses: Severely limited scope: only mathematics domain and pairwise evaluation—findings may not generalize to other domains and evaluation formats where judges are widely deployed
No methodological novelty: applies only existing training methods (SFT, DPO) without proposing new solutions to identified problems
Simplistic generator strength definition based solely on pass@1 accuracy without capturing style, reasoning patterns, or error modes; arbitrary weak/strong threshold lacks justification

Question generalization findings are incomplete: large 2-10% performance drops on unseen questions are documented but not investigated or addressed; no explanation for why larger models generalize worse
Continual learning analysis is underdeveloped: only 1 arbitrary additional epoch tested, mixed backward-compatibility results without explanation, no comparison to alternative adaptation methods
Limited mechanistic insight: shows WHAT happens but minimally explores WHY (e.g., why DPO enables better backward compatibility, what linguistic differences drive shifts)

Experimental rigor issues: no error bars or confidence intervals despite small test sets, no statistical significance testing, different judge training compositions per base model complicate cross-comparison, pass@1 calculation sensitivity unexplored
Missing baselines and comparisons to zero-shot judges, other domain adaptation techniques, or ensemble approaches
Predictable findings: that finetuned judges overfit to training distributions is unsurprising; no novel solutions beyond retraining and basic continual learning

Incomplete analysis leaves practitioners without clear actionable guidance: unclear when to use continual learning vs. retraining from scratch; absolute performance sufficiency under distribution shift not discussed

strengths: Addresses practically important problem in LLM judge deployment as generators evolve over time
Clean and well-motivated dual-distribution framework (Q × R × R) enabling systematic analysis of different distribution shifts
Comprehensive and careful experimental design across multiple models (3 base judges), training recipes (SFT, DPO, SFT+DPO), and evaluation dimensions with appropriate controls
Clear, actionable findings with direct practical implications: future-proofing is challenging, strong-trained judges are backward-compatible, continual learning helps
Well-structured presentation with clear research questions, good motivation, and effective visualizations
weaknesses: Severely limited scope: entire evaluation confined to single domain (mathematics/DeepScaleR); generalization to other critical domains (NLG, code, retrieval) unknown
Limited generator coverage and weak/strong definition based only on pass@1; missing sensitivity analysis and exploration of alternative generator properties or distribution shift variations
Shallow analysis of question generalization (Section 5.4): identifies large performance drops but doesn't investigate underlying causes or propose solutions despite practical importance
Only DPO tested for continual learning due to compute constraints; simple strategy (1 epoch) unexplored; SFT/SFT+DPO continual learning entirely absent
No statistical rigor: missing confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests despite ~2.5K evaluation samples; some reported differences (0.7-1.1 pp) may not be significant
No methodological contributions: uses standard training approaches without innovation; framework is useful but not novel; limited engagement with domain adaptation or robust ML literature
Artificial dataset construction: pairs always have one correct/incorrect response; generalization to realistic scenarios (both mostly-correct or mostly-incorrect) unexplored

Limited solution space discussed: identifies problems but offers minimal actionable solutions beyond continual learning; no discussion of regularization, uncertainty quantification, or online learning approaches
Expected findings with limited novelty: core result (old judges fail on new data) is intuitive; confirms rather than reveals surprising insights
Reproducibility concerns: computationally expensive to reproduce (multiple generator responses + GPT-4o teacher); no mention of code/data release

strengths: Addresses a practically important and understudied problem about LLM judge robustness across model generations, with clear real-world relevance
Proposes an elegant dual-distribution framework that cleanly separates question and response distributions, providing a principled way to reason about distribution shifts in evaluation

Comprehensive and carefully designed experiments: two diverse datasets (reasoning and knowledge), three backbone models, three training recipes, proper train-test splits, and thoughtful handling of self-bias

Clear and consistent empirical findings across settings: universal future-proofing failure, superior backward-compatibility with DPO, poor question generalization, and domain-dependent severity of distribution shift
Well-executed empirical work with good reproducibility: extensive implementation details, clear metrics, informative visualizations, and complete results tables
Provides actionable insights for practitioners: judges must be retrained on newer responses, DPO yields larger gains than SFT, and continual learning offers balanced adaptation
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: primarily applies existing training methods (SFT, DPO) to a new problem without proposing new algorithms or techniques to address identified challenges
Diagnostic rather than prescriptive: paper identifies problems convincingly but offers limited solutions beyond retraining and continual learning, which is only partially explored

Incomplete failure analysis: lacks investigation into why judges fail (e.g., what characteristics of strong responses cause degradation, error case studies, sensitivity analyses), and surprising findings like SFT's better generalization to unseen questions are not explained

Experimental gaps: continual learning only tested on DeepScaleR+DPO due to compute constraints with limited hyperparameter exploration; question generalization solutions not proposed; no investigation of intermediate model capabilities or gradual degradation
Missing statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, significance tests, or multiple runs reported; some performance differences appear marginal without uncertainty quantification

Limited scope and generalizability: only pairwise evaluation on datasets with verifiable answers; domain effects differ substantially between math and knowledge tasks but not deeply analyzed; findings may not transfer to open-ended generation evaluation
Lack of theoretical insights: primarily empirical with limited explanation for why DPO outperforms SFT for backward-compatibility or why question generalization fails consistently
Missing comparisons: no comparison with zero-shot frontier model judges or recent RL-based judge training approaches mentioned in related work

strengths: Addresses a timely, practical problem relevant to practitioners deploying judge models in rapidly evolving LLM ecosystems
Clean conceptual framework (dual-distribution formalization) providing principled way to decompose question vs. response distribution shifts
Comprehensive experimental design spanning two datasets, multiple backbone models, multiple training recipes, and systematic evaluation conditions
Consistent findings across DeepScaleR and MMLU-Pro datasets suggest robustness despite domain differences
Well-written with clear presentation, informative figures, and transparent experimental setup
Concrete operationalized metrics (FutureProof, RefreshAdvantage, etc.) that could be useful for practitioners
weaknesses: Limited novelty: primarily an empirical characterization study with somewhat expected findings—judges degrade on stronger responses, retraining helps, backward-compatibility exceeds future-proofing

Lack of actionable solutions: paper diagnoses problems but only proposes obvious remedies (retrain, include questions in training); no exploration of sophisticated adaptation strategies (domain adaptation, meta-learning, few-shot, uncertainty-driven retraining)
Incomplete continual learning experiments: only DPO tested due to compute constraints, single-epoch training, mixed/inconsistent results without clear understanding of when/why it works
Data construction bias inadequately addressed: selection enriches for medium-difficulty borderline questions (Figure 9), potentially affecting generalization in unexplored ways
Shallow mechanistic analysis: paper reports numbers without explaining why (e.g., why DPO outperforms SFT on RefreshAdvantage? why larger models worse at question generalization?)
Limited scope: only pairwise evaluation tested; only 2 datasets (math + MCQ knowledge); only open-source instruction-tuned generators; only GPT-4o as teacher model
Missing statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, significance testing, or multiple random seeds reported; no ablations on key design choices (teacher model, β parameters, epochs)
No human validation of whether improved metrics actually matter for downstream use; all evaluation against automated metrics only
Weak/strong binary clustering is artificial—real model improvement is continuous; no exploration of extrapolation beyond this gap or intermediate model performance
Incomplete exploration of related literature: limited engagement with domain adaptation, out-of-distribution generalization, and curriculum learning

strengths: Addresses an important and timely practical problem relevant to real-world LLM evaluation systems
Introduces a clean and useful dual-distribution framework (Q × R) for systematically analyzing judge robustness to distribution shifts
Comprehensive experimental setup spanning two datasets, multiple backbone models, three training recipes, with careful controls for self-bias and positional bias
Clear, well-motivated metrics (FutureProof, RefreshAdvantage, BackCompatibility, QuestionGen) directly tied to practical concerns
Consistent and robust findings across complementary datasets (reasoning-intensive vs knowledge-intensive), strengthening generalizability
Well-designed experiments with natural weak/strong clustering separated by 0.13-0.16 gaps in Pass@1, reducing threshold arbitrariness
Actionable insights: DPO outperforms SFT for updates, backward-compatibility is easier than future-proofing, continual learning provides balanced adaptation
Thorough documentation enabling reproducibility with detailed hyperparameters, full result tables, and extensive appendix
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: primarily empirical analysis of existing training methods without new algorithms or theoretical contributions

Solutions offered are superficial and underdeveloped: continual learning tested only with DPO using 1 additional epoch; no principled explanation for why it works; no exploration of alternative approaches (meta-learning, mixture models, etc.)

Weak statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, significance tests, or error bars; single runs only; small evaluation sets (2.5K) may have high variance; unclear if reported differences are statistically significant
Lack of mechanistic understanding: asymmetry between weak-to-strong and strong-to-weak shifts is striking but unexplained; missing error analysis of what causes future-proofing failures
Evaluation limited to pairwise judgment format; generalizability to other evaluation paradigms (ratings, ranking, open-ended) unclear, limiting practical impact
Restricted to verifiable-answer datasets (exact math, multiple-choice); findings may not transfer to open-ended generation or subjective quality assessment
Question generalization results somewhat expected; limited investigation into why judges fail or concrete solutions beyond generic suggestion to 'expose judges to target questions'
Dataset selection bias underexplored: filtering for mixed correct/incorrect responses creates medium-difficulty concentration (Figure 9); impact on generalizability not quantified
Incomplete continual learning experiments: restricted to DeepScaleR due to compute constraints; limited exploration of hyperparameters (β results only in appendix); SFT+DPO not tested
Insufficient ablations and comparisons: no analysis of data size effects, training mixing strategies, or sensitivity to question/response overlap; causality inference remains correlational
